approach_variants.name: Eldorado Creek climbers' path to Inspiration Glacier high camp
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the talus is bare
approach_variants.hours: 5-7 to high camp, 3-5 more to the summit
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount roughly 20 miles to the Eldorado parking area at about 2,100 ft. The first ten miles are paved; the rest is gravel and washboard.

The path does not leave from the parking area. Walk back down the road about 90 feet and look for the log (historically a large single log, sometimes a clump of trees) spanning the Cascade River. The crossing shifts year to year and is slick when wet — a handline is worth carrying for a party that is not confident on a log. On the far bank walk perpendicular to the river roughly 100 feet to pick up the boot path.

The path climbs steeply and relentlessly through old-growth timber with no water, gaining about 1,500 ft before it breaks out into the boulder field. Follow cairns and flagging up the boulders, staying climber's right so you do not cross Eldorado Creek unnecessarily. The boulder field is universally described as the worst part of the trip, and worse on the way down with a heavy pack.

Above the boulders the ground eases into Eldorado Creek Basin (roughly 5,400-5,600 ft, about 3 miles and 3,300 ft from the car), a common first camp. To continue, climb onto the rocky ridge at about 6,100 ft and drop a few hundred feet on the far side into Roush Creek Basin (6,100-6,400 ft, running water). From Roush, broken talus and slabs lead onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier; rope up here. Moderate glacier slopes lead to high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration saddle around 7,500-7,800 ft.

Overnight stays need a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. Eldorado is a high-use cross-country zone; there is an advance lottery and reservations on Recreation.gov, but permits for the areas off Cascade River Road (Eldorado, Boston Basin, Cascade Pass) must be picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no rock start on this route — the climbing is the summit snow arete, and finding it means finding one gap on an otherwise featureless glacier.

From high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration saddle the Inspiration Glacier runs away nearly flat to the west. Cross it aiming for the obvious low gap in Eldorado's lower East Ridge, universally called 'The Gap' in trip reports. Once you have stepped through the gap you are on the East Ridge; before that you are still on flat glacier.

The confirmation underfoot is that the ground stops being flat and becomes a defined crest, with glacier falling away on both sides rather than one. From the gap, go a short way further up onto the snow until a distinct ramp leads leftward/rightward onto the ridge crest proper — parties consistently report a gentle ramp reaching the base of the knife edge from its far right side. That ramp, and the point where the crest narrows so that both sides drop, is the base of the climbing.

The common error is stopping short: the flat Inspiration is genuinely disorienting in cloud, several trip reports describe an hour of whiteout walking to reach the gap, and parties drift too low into crevassed glacier instead of holding the line to the low point on the skyline. Take and hold a bearing from camp. Later in the season the crest melts out and parties move onto the steeper snow slope to the right of the bare ridge, where crevasses open — early season the same crest can be broad enough to skin.

Stay roped on the ridge. It is not a rock ridge you have escaped the glacier onto; the line travels back onto glacier and crevasses exist on the crest itself.
hazards: Cascade River log crossing — slick when wet, position shifts year to year
Boulder field is the crux of the walk, worse descending under a heavy pack
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration Glaciers, worsening as the day warms
Featureless flat glacier — whiteout navigation to The Gap
Exposed summit knife-edge; crevasses on the ridge crest itself

approach_variants.name: Late-spring snow cover (skis or boots)
approach_variants.notes:
In late spring the upper approach is continuous snow and the boulder field problem largely disappears, which is why many parties prefer this window. It does not make the whole approach snow: a late-May park report described the route as snow-free until just before Eldorado Basin was gained around 5,000 ft, with the boulder fields completely melted out — so expect a dry, steep forest climb first and snow only above.

Ski parties commonly carry ski boots and walk the forest section in approach or running shoes, switching over at snow line.

The trade is avalanche exposure. Large avalanches sweep parts of this route in winter and spring, and Cascade River Road itself can be buried by avalanche debris miles below the trailhead in a heavy year, adding road miles before you even start.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same gap in the lower East Ridge, but early season it is broader and more forgiving: the ridge is wide, sometimes wide enough to skin, and the knife edge that defines the route later in the summer may not have formed yet. Do not treat a wide, easy crest as evidence you are in the wrong place — the landmark is still The Gap, the low point on the ridge skyline reached by crossing the flat Inspiration.
hazards: Avalanche paths across the approach and the road in spring
Snow-bridged creek channels in the lower basins — parties have punched through
Road may be closed or buried well below the trailhead

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass Trail and Sahale Arm to Sahale Glacier Camp
approach_variants.hours: 4-5 to camp, about 2 more to the summit
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road runs about 22-23 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead, a large lot at road's end at 3,600 ft. This is the only approach on this list that is on maintained trail almost the whole way.

The Cascade Pass Trail switchbacks up through old-growth timber — roughly 35 switchbacks, about 1,800 ft in the first two miles — then eases through meadows to Cascade Pass at about 5,400 ft, 3.5-3.7 miles in. At the pass take the left (north) fork for Sahale Arm and switchback up the open ridge crest, about another 2.1-2.2 miles and 2,200 ft, to Sahale Glacier Camp at roughly 7,200-7,600 ft — rock-walled tent pads on the moraine, and the NPS-permitted high camp.

Water is reliable at the creek crossings low on the trail, at Doubtful Lake (a signed spur, about a mile and 1,000 ft down and back) and from snowmelt near Sahale Glacier Camp early and mid season. Sources dry up late summer, so fill before the long switchback climb.

Above camp the Sahale Glacier is small and low-angle by North Cascades standards but should still be treated as a glacier — rope up rather than assuming it out.

Overnight camping is quota-limited and needs a North Cascades backcountry permit picked up in person at Marblemount.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing is the summit pyramid above the glacier, and the mistake to avoid is attacking it straight on.

From the top of the glacier you arrive under the southwest side of the summit block. Do not start up the steepest ground directly in front of you. Trend right toward the notch, then onto the north/east side of the block — the correct line corkscrews around the peak rather than going up it. You should find yourself on a system of solid but increasingly exposed class 3 ledges, not on a face.

The last confirmation is a short class 4 move — about twenty feet of it, one awkward crack or chimney-like exit that puts you through a notch in the summit rocks onto the top. There is a fixed rappel station at that spot, and finding a fixed anchor is the clearest proof from the ground that you are on the standard line and not a variation.

The trap is the dihedral. Left of the standard notch there is a steeper dihedral feature that reads as the obvious line; it goes at fourth to low fifth class on loose rock and wants gear. If you are looking at a clean-cut corner rather than a rubble ledge that leads around and right, you are on the harder variation.

In poor visibility: the block is small and unmistakable once you are at it, so the navigation problem is the glacier, not the rock. Late season the glacier surface is cut by meltwater runnels that look like crevasses and crevasses that look like runnels — parties report going up and climber's right, climbing diagonally across the gullies, because that side reads more reliably.
hazards: Loose rock on the summit block, with parties directly above and below on a popular route
Exposed class 3-4 scrambling — many parties belay the last section
Meltwater runnels on the glacier disguising real crevasses late season
Water sources dry by late summer between the trailhead and Doubtful Lake

approach_variants.name: Car-to-car day push
approach_variants.notes:
Because the approach is on maintained trail to about 7,200 ft, Sahale is regularly done in a single long day from the trailhead, which sidesteps the quota-limited high camp entirely. The trade is that you carry glacier gear the whole 6 miles up and 6 miles down, and you meet the summit block later in the day when it is busiest and the snow is softest.

Nothing about the line changes; only the logistics do. If the permit lottery has closed you out of Sahale Glacier Camp, this is the fallback rather than a different route.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical to the camp version — the pyramid above the top of the Sahale Glacier, gained by trending right to the notch and following ledges around the block to the short class 4 exit at the fixed rappel station.
hazards: Long day with glacier gear carried the full distance
Arriving at the summit block in the afternoon queue

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin climbers' trail and Quien Sabe Glacier
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-4 to camp, 3-4 more to the col
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the Boston Basin fork at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft. There is no trailhead sign — it is an unmarked pullout, so watch the odometer rather than looking for signage.

Walk the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile to a mile, past the derelict mine site, with almost no elevation gain. The point people miss is where the climbers' trail leaves the roadbed sharply to the right and goes straight up; it is cairned and flagged but easy to walk past.

Above that the path is steep and unmaintained, switchbacking through forest and a brushy old slide path with deadfall, and crossing four small streams over roughly the next half mile — that is the last reliable water before camp, so fill there. Treeline comes at about 5,300 ft. Low camp sits on heather benches around 5,300-5,700 ft; the higher camp on a meadow knoll at about 6,200-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day.

From camp, stay on climber's left toward the left side of Sharkfin Tower, rope up around 6,700 ft, and make a rising traverse under the cliffs below Sharkfin onto a flatter part of the Quien Sabe, then pick a line up the steeper section. Two common lines (one further left, one more direct) merge partway up.

Boston Basin is a cross-country zone; overnight permits are picked up in person at Marblemount. Biting flies are notorious here in midsummer.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The rock climbing begins at the Boston-Sahale col, and everything below it is glacier work.

The navigational problem on the way up is the bergschrund, at roughly 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft where large open crevasses flank the route on both sides late season. Late in the year the standard solution is to traverse climber's right to end-run the schrund, then cut back up and left above it to the col — a party that pushes straight up the fall line into the schrund is not off route so much as too early in the season for that line.

You know you are at the col because the glacier ends against a defined saddle in the rock ridge and the ground on the far side drops away toward Boston Peak. This is where parties unrope and coil.

From the col the route is the ridge: it steepens, then widens, then narrows to an exposed class 3-4 knife edge. At the high point of that ridge the false summit comes into view ahead of you — that view is the confirmation that you have done the ridge section correctly and are approaching the summit block. The block is then finished as on the Sahale Glacier route, on ledges around the east side to a short class 4 exit at a fixed rappel station.

In poor visibility the col itself is the reliable target: it is the only low saddle at the top of the glacier, and the ridge beyond it cannot be confused with glacier travel.
hazards: Missing the sharp right turn off the mine roadbed onto the climbers' trail
Bergschrund at roughly 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft, open both sides late season
Rockfall from the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower during the rising traverse
Exposed knife-edge ridge above the col
Biting flies in Boston Basin in midsummer

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — early season, snow gully
approach_variants.season: Jun-mid Jul, while the approach gully still holds snow
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-3 to camp, about 2.5 more to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as everything else in Boston Basin: the unsigned pullout on Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft, the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile, then the sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. Four stream crossings, then treeline at about 5,300 ft. Low camp on heather benches at 5,300-5,700 ft, higher camp on the knoll at about 6,300-6,400 ft.

From camp, skirt climber's left of the Quien Sabe Glacier and gain it relatively high, then rope up and traverse east/climber's right along the top of the glacier several hundred feet until you are directly beneath the tower.

Early season the approach gully is snow, around 35 degrees, and is the pleasant version of this approach — crampons and an axe, straightforward booting. A bergschrund or seracs can bar the direct entry; class 3-4 slabs on the left provide an alternate way in that rejoins the gully about a hundred feet up.

Do the identification work on the walk in, not at the base. The whole sequence — glacier, gully, terrace and notch — is visible from the lower Boston Basin trail and from camp. Look at it in good light while you still have perspective on it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the most consequential base-finding problem on this list, and it has killed people.

The correct line: from a position on the glacier directly below the tower — not past it — a single gully breaks through the steep rock band. Follow it up to a snow patch or sloping terrace at the base of the tower. From that terrace, a short second gully leads to a notch, and the notch is the start of the Southeast Ridge. Some parties also describe a snow gully west of the tower that gives access to that same wide bench below the objective.

The test to apply before committing: does this gully put me on a terrace directly under the fin? If you are climbing a gully that trends away from being underneath the tower, you are in the wrong one. Being on rock is not evidence of being on route — there are similar-looking gullies here.

On 10 July 2005 a six-person party crossed the glacier, walked past the standard access gully and climbed a similar-looking gully further along. The traverse back toward the correct line put them under rockfall, which struck a climber; during the retreat rappel a natural boulder anchor failed. Three died and a fourth was seriously injured. Every subsequent description of this approach leads with the same instruction: identify the correct gully.

Carry a beta photo or a GPS track. In cloud, when you cannot see the fin above you, this approach should not be committed to on guesswork.
hazards: Wrong-gully error — the defining hazard of this approach, with a fatal precedent
Bergschrund or seracs barring the direct gully entry
Rockfall in the gully, natural and from parties above
Poor natural anchors — a boulder anchor failure caused the 2005 fatalities
Crevasses on the Quien Sabe traverse

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — late season, dry gully
approach_variants.season: Aug-Sep, once the gully has melted out
approach_variants.notes:
The walk in is identical. What changes is the gully: by late summer the snow is gone and it is loose scree and rubble, manageable but tedious and much more prone to knocking rock onto whoever is below. Trekking poles replace crampons.

The other late-season change is the moat where the glacier meets rock at the gully's base, which opens up as the season goes on and can require a committing step or a short awkward move onto rock.

One recorded late-season day trip left town at 4am, was in Boston Basin by about 8:30am, traversed underneath the tower to find the approach gully, and reached the notch before 11am.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The identification rule does not change: the correct gully is the one directly beneath the tower that delivers you onto the sloping terrace at the fin's base, followed by a short gully to the notch that begins the Southeast Ridge.

Late season it is arguably harder to be sure, because the snow that made the gully obvious from a distance has gone and several dry rubble chutes look alike from the glacier. Rely on the view from lower down: the gully, terrace and notch are all visible from the approach trail and from camp, so fix the line in your head before you lose the perspective.

Descent parties commonly rappel part of the route and then off rock to the west of the approach gully, so a fixed station west of your gully is a supporting sign you are in the right corridor — but it is a weaker signal than the terrace itself.
hazards: Wrong-gully error, harder to rule out once the snow has gone
Loose scree and climber-triggered rockfall in the gully
Open moat at the glacier-rock junction
Rockfall from parties rappelling the descent line

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin, rising traverse to the Taboo Glacier
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-4 to high camp, about 1-2 more to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount, directly opposite Johannesburg), take the old Diamond Mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right turn onto the steep climbers' trail. Four small creek crossings, treeline about 5,300 ft, low camp 5,300-5,500 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft.

From high camp leave any semblance of trail and make a rising traverse to the northwest, holding roughly the 6,200 ft contour across talus, tundra and slab steps. You pass beneath the south spur of Forbidden Peak and cross a prominent rock rib below the cliffs, with the Taboo Glacier coming into view above.

Gain the Taboo Glacier on its climber's-left side and follow it up. Some parties skip the summit-day traverse entirely by carrying up the Taboo and camping at about 7,100 ft directly beneath Torment's southeast face at the foot of the couloir.

This traverse is the part that gets people lost in cloud. It is open, uniform ground with no trail, and in early season the creek channels are buried and there is avalanche exposure across it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at a prominent notch in the South Ridge, at the top of the east couloir that comes off the Taboo Glacier — and the couloir, not the notch, is what you are hunting for from the glacier.

Follow the Taboo up until a deep gully or couloir breaks through the rock band on your left. It is a definite break, not a weakness in a face. A bergschrund or moat guards its bottom; this crossing is the standard place parties stop, put the sharp end on, and it has been the site of a fatal accident, so it is not a formality. Early season it is snow-bridged; late season it is wide open and the couloir above it may be completely melted out to rock.

From the schrund, scramble roughly a hundred feet of loose class 3-4 up the gully to the notch. You are at the base of the route when you are standing in a notch on the ridge crest with Torment Basin dropping away on the west side and the Taboo Glacier below you to the east. If you have gained rock but there is no crest and no view down the far side, you have gone up a break in the rock band rather than the couloir.

The late-season workaround is worth knowing, because it removes the moat problem entirely: instead of crossing onto the ridge at the notch, cross the South Ridge at about 6,600 ft and gain the ridge from the Torment Basin side. Adjacent scrambling variations that avoid the snow couloir and reach the same notch are also described.

Be aware this gully is a queue on a busy weekend — parties commonly wait below the schrund for the group above to clear the loose class 3-4 rather than climb underneath them.
hazards: Bergschrund or moat at the base of the couloir — fatal accident on record
Loose class 3-4 rock in the gully with parties above
Featureless traverse from Boston Basin, easy to lose in whiteout
Early-season avalanche exposure on the traverse; buried creek channels
Couloir can be entirely melted out late season

approach_variants.name: Torment Basin climbers' path
approach_variants.notes:
A separate and much less-used way in that skips Boston Basin altogether. Drive Cascade River Road only about 20 miles — roughly a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead — and look for the climbers' path starting about fifty feet upstream of the bridge over the Cascade River.

It is a steep, hard climb on a boot path that is mostly easy to follow up into Torment Basin, but despite decades of traffic some sections stay genuinely brushy. It puts you on the west side of the South Ridge rather than the east.

The reason to use it is the moat: from the Torment Basin side the South Ridge can be gained at about 6,600 ft without crossing the moat at the top of the Taboo Glacier, which is the late-season crux of the standard approach. It is also the shorter drive.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming from Torment Basin you meet the South Ridge from the west, so you do not arrive at the notch from below — you gain the crest at about 6,600 ft and follow it. The confirmation is the crest itself and the Taboo Glacier appearing below on the east side once you are on it. This is the same ridge the standard approach reaches at the notch above the couloir, entered lower down.
hazards: Brushy sections on a steep unmaintained boot path
Less-travelled approach — fewer parties, less current beta on conditions

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin high camp and the Taboo Glacier
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-4 to high camp, about 1-2 more to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
The traverse starts by climbing Torment's South Ridge, so the approach is the South Ridge approach. From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount), take the old mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. Four creek crossings, treeline at about 5,300 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft — call it 2.5-3 miles and 3,000-3,300 ft from the car.

From high camp traverse the upper basin northwest at roughly the 6,200 ft contour, beneath Forbidden's south spur, crossing a rock rib and a couple of snowmelt channels, heading for the toe of the Taboo Glacier and the lower South Ridge.

Because the traverse is long and committing, many parties instead carry over and camp at about 7,100 ft on the Taboo directly under Torment's southeast face at the foot of the east couloir, which turns a very long day into a reasonable one. Others bivy on the ridge partway across.

Overnight permits for Boston Basin are picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The traverse's start is the same notch that starts the South Ridge, and finding it is a glacier problem, not a rock problem.

Rope up at the toe of the Taboo and follow the glacier up on its climber's-left side, watching for crevasses. You are looking for the one deep gully that breaks the rock band on the left — the east couloir. A bergschrund and a moat sit at its base; the moat where the glacier pulls away from rock can require a short awkward move onto rock, and this crossing is where a picket, axe and crampons for the leader earn their weight.

Above the schrund, scramble roughly a hundred feet of loose class 3-4 to the notch. Standing in the notch you are on the crest with Torment Basin dropping away to the west and the Taboo below to the east — that two-sided view is the confirmation that you are at the base of the climbing and not partway up a blind break in the rock band.

Later in the season, when the moat is bad, parties cross the South Ridge at about 6,600 ft and gain it from the Torment Basin side instead. Adjacent scrambling lines that avoid the snow couloir and rejoin the same notch are also described.

The whole basin-to-glacier traverse is genuinely easy to lose in a whiteout — it is uniform open ground with no trail — so if you cannot see the Taboo, do not start the traverse on dead reckoning alone.
hazards: Moat and bergschrund at the foot of the east couloir — fatal accident on record
Loose class 3-4 gully with parties above
Whiteout navigation across the basin-to-glacier traverse
Early-season avalanche exposure and buried creek crossings
Biting flies in Boston Basin in midsummer

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass trailhead, river ford and the snow finger
approach_variants.notes:
This is the shortest approach on this list and one of the shortest in the range — the wall stands directly above the Cascade Pass parking lot.

From the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft (or from the hairpin turn just below it), walk back down the road roughly a quarter mile, then scramble down a dirt and brush embankment to the Cascade River. Ford it. This is glacial meltwater and it runs highest in the afternoon on hot days, so an early start helps on the way in and the timing of your return matters as much.

Beyond the river, push through a short stretch of brush and climb up and over the terminal moraine and debris below the northeast face, picking up a boot path, and trend toward the obvious snow finger. Roughly an hour car to base, half an hour for a fast party.

The brevity is deceptive. Above the snow there is no trail at all, and Johannesburg has a long history of parties returning one to two days late. Expect 8-12 hours from the base to the bivy around 7,100 ft.

Water: the river at the ford and seasonal seeps low on the buttress. There is none once you are on rock.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route begins at the top of the snow finger at about 3,500 ft, and the finger is the thing you are navigating to — a distinct tongue of snow leading up and rightward toward the buttress, obvious from the moraine.

You are at the base when you run out of snow at the top of the finger and the only way on is up and right into vegetation. There is no rock start, no cairn and no anchor: the transition is snow to alder. The first climbing is hand-over-hand up alder in a mossy streambed, then steep turf and heather, with short sections of tunnelling through subalpine trees, trending right the whole time to gain the buttress crest at roughly 5,000-5,500 ft.

The error to avoid is going straight up. Above the snow finger the natural-looking continuation is the gully or couloir line above it, which holds rockfall; the route leaves the snow at the finger's top and works rightward onto the rib that bounds it. If you are still in a drainage rather than climbing a rib, you have gone up rather than right.

Route-finding through the brush and cliff bands stays tricky well above the base — a good line exists through the vegetation onto steep heather and class 4 rock, but you will not find it by feel in poor visibility. Rope drag from the bushes is bad enough that parties pitch it short or simul.

A blunt honesty note: in under a mile of horizontal distance you gain roughly 3,500-4,600 ft. There is nothing gentle about this base, and standing at the river you are already looking at the whole thing.
hazards: Cascade River ford — glacial melt, peaks in hot afternoons, worst on the return
Loose moraine and rockfall in the snow finger and the gully above it
No trail above the snow; sustained brush and heather route-finding
Long history of parties overdue by one to two days
No water above the low seeps

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass trailhead to the couloir apron
approach_variants.season: May-Jun, while the Sill Glacier snow is still continuous
approach_variants.notes:
Effectively no approach at all. From the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft, walk back down the road — accounts range from a quarter mile to just under a mile depending on where you drop in — then descend a dirt and brush embankment into the valley and cross the Cascade River. In spring the river is often still snow-covered where you cross.

Over the terminal moraine and a snowfield, and within about twenty minutes of dropping off the road you are putting crampons on at the apron at roughly 3,300 ft. From there it is about 3,000 ft of continuous booting to the Cascade-Johannesburg col.

In a big snow year Cascade River Road may be gated well below the trailhead — one ski party found it gated at mile 18 but snow-free to the last hairpin, and used bikes for the road section. Budget for that possibility rather than assuming you can drive to the end.

Season is the whole decision on this route. Early season is when the snow is continuous. As the Sill Glacier breaks up, the snow in the couloir goes discontinuous where it narrows near the hanging glacier and the breaks turn into a series of separate problems; by mid to late summer it is broken and considerably more hazardous.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is easy to find and the hard part is judging it, which is unusual on this list.

The couloir is the obvious deep gash in the skyline directly between Cascade Peak on the left and Johannesburg on the right, and it is in full view from the trailhead parking lot and the last road switchbacks. Identify it from the car, in daylight, before you drop into the valley — this is the one approach here where you get a complete view of your line before committing to it, and you should use that.

On the ground, you are at the base when the moraine and brush end and you step onto a continuous snow apron at around 3,300 ft. From the apron, looking up the couloir, the line is unambiguous — there are no alternative gullies to confuse it with.

What you cannot see from the apron is the part that matters. The couloir narrows higher up near the obvious hanging glacier, and that is where the snow goes discontinuous as the season progresses. A base that looks perfect in July tells you nothing about the middle. Judge continuity from the road, where the whole 3,000 ft is in view, and be willing to turn around at the car.

The honest caveat carried by every source that describes this line: it is the most direct route on Johannesburg and also the most dangerous, guarded by overhead rock and ice fall that is hard to justify once the snow is not continuous.
hazards: Rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier over the whole couloir
Discontinuous snow where the couloir narrows, worsening through the season
Cascade River crossing — snow-bridged in spring, a ford later
Spring wet-slide activity in a 3,000 ft snow chute
Road may be gated miles below the trailhead in a heavy snow year

approach_variants.name: Up the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir to the C-J col
approach_variants.season: May-Jun for continuous snow in the couloir
approach_variants.notes:
The East Ridge is reached from the Cascade-Johannesburg col, and the direct way there is to climb the couloir that names it. The start is the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft: walk back down the road, drop the embankment into the valley, cross the Cascade River, and go over the moraine onto the couloir apron at roughly 3,300 ft — about twenty minutes from leaving the road. Then roughly 3,000 ft of booting to the col.

This is the fast way and the dangerous way. The couloir carries rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier above, and the snow goes discontinuous where it narrows as the season progresses, so it is an early-season proposition.

The East Ridge by way of the C-J Couloir was first climbed in 1938 and is the most-used line on the peak; it and the other routes finishing on the south side are mostly scrambling.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the climbing is the Cascade-Johannesburg col itself — the notch at the top of the couloir, with Johannesburg on one side and Cascade Peak on the other. There is no ambiguity about arriving: the snow ends against the saddle and the ground drops away on the far side.

From the col the East Ridge is the crest running west toward Cascade Peak's summit, on your right as you top out of the couloir. Published descriptions of the ground above are thin and consistent on one point only: route-finding is complicated, exposure is significant, and loose rock is everywhere. Parties commonly climb it unroped while carrying a harness in case they want a belay.

There are numerous rappel stations scattered around this area from previous parties, and reports note that some of them need improving before use — treat a found anchor as information, not as confirmation you are on route.
hazards: Rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier in the couloir
Discontinuous couloir snow after early season
Loose rock and complicated route-finding on the ridge above the col
Existing rappel stations of unknown quality

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass, Mixup Arm and the Cache Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
The walking way in, avoiding the couloir entirely. Follow the Cascade Pass Trail from the trailhead at 3,600 ft for 3.5-3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at roughly 5,400 ft. At the pass, near the benches, turn right and pick up the obvious climbers' path onto Mixup Arm.

Cross Mixup Arm and traverse and descend rightward until you reach the Cache Glacier — the described landmark is a seasonal waterfall, past which you turn right and ascend the lobe of the Cache.

One party using this side reported a long sidehill traverse beneath the Triplets and Cascade Peak, camping in a meadow below the C-J col at about 6,200 ft. That camp puts you at the base of the East Ridge for the following morning without ever entering the couloir.

Early season the traverse across Mixup's flank is snow-covered with a poor runout; late season Cache Col and the glacier edges can moat out.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Approaching from this side you arrive at the C-J col or the meadows just below it rather than climbing up to it, so the confirmation is positional: the col is the saddle between Johannesburg and Cascade Peak at the head of the couloir, and from the meadow camp below it the East Ridge runs up on the Cascade Peak side.

Gunsight Notch — the prominent notch to the west of Cache Col — is the published portal from the Cache Glacier side for Mix-Up, the Triplets and Cascade Peak, so a party approaching Cascade Peak from the Cache rather than from the col is aiming at that notch instead. The snow tongue to Gunsight Notch is short, about a hundred feet, but steep at roughly 50-65 degrees, with bergschrunds on either side of it dropping ten to fifteen feet to a rock floor, and rockfall in tight quarters between snow and rock.
hazards: Snow-covered traverse on Mixup's flank with bad runout in early season
Cache Col and glacier margins moat out late season
Steep short snow tongue and flanking bergschrunds at Gunsight Notch
Rockfall in the confined ground between snow and rock at the notch

wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge._note: Cascade Peak is thinly documented compared with its neighbours. The C-J col and the couloir approach are well corroborated because they are shared with Johannesburg; the ground on the East Ridge above the col, and the Cache Glacier side approach, rest on few accounts. Nothing has been written here about the ridge itself beyond what those accounts state.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass, Mixup Arm bench and the Cache Glacier
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; access gets harder through August as the Cache Glacier recedes
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road runs about 22-23 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead at 3,600 ft. Follow the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.5-3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to the pass at roughly 5,400 ft. There is no reliable water at the pass beyond seasonal snowmelt, so fill at a creek crossing lower down.

At the pass, near the benches, turn right (south) onto the obvious climbers' path — do not continue on the maintained trail toward Stehekin. The path bends south-southeast and makes a rising traverse across heather and talus on the flanks of Mixup Arm and Mixup Peak's east slopes at roughly the 6,000 ft contour, crossing a minor spur ridge.

This traverse crosses steep snow gullies that hold snow well into summer. In early season the runout is bad — a slip has a drop of several hundred feet below it — so an ice axe and genuine comfort on firm snow traverses are the entry requirement, not optional extras.

Continue to the toe of the Cache Glacier at about 6,000-6,200 ft. The described landmark is a seasonal waterfall: walk past it, turn right, and ascend the lobe of the Cache.

Camping is prohibited at Cascade Pass and on Mixup Arm, so this is either a long car-to-car day of 7-9 hours to the summit, or you continue past the notch to established sites at Kool-Aid Lake (about 6,120 ft) or near Cache Col.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are two notches at the head of the Cache Glacier on Mixup's east side, and picking the wrong one is the standard mistake.

A U-shaped notch sits on the left and a V-shaped notch on the right. The East Face is accessed from the V-notch. It is common — and accepted — to go up through the U-notch on the left and wrap around the back side to reach the V, so being at the U is not a failure, but starting to climb from it is.

Gunsight Notch, the prominent notch west of Cache Col, is the portal that serves Mix-Up, the Triplets and Cascade Peak, and the snow tongue leading to it is short, about a hundred feet, but steep at roughly 50-65 degrees. Bergschrunds flank the tongue on either side, dropping ten to fifteen feet to a rock floor, and the ground between the snow and the rock is wet, tight and swept by rockfall.

From the south side of the notch the sequence is specific and is your confirmation: go west about 100 ft down a side gully, then ascend northwest up a wide, loose gully to a saddle. At that saddle the White Staircase begins — an easy, exposed class 3 staircase of pale grey rock on the right-hand side of the large summit pyramid. If you are looking at a grey staircase-like ramp on the right side of the pyramid, you are exactly where you should be.

The hardest and dirtiest climbing on the whole approach is the first fifty feet out of the moat where the glacier meets rock — perhaps mid-fifth on loose ground. That difficulty is itself a tell: if the entry felt trivial, check that you have actually crossed the moat at the right place.

Season matters for this specifically. As the Cache Glacier recedes, getting to the notch has been getting harder year on year, and by August the moat can be the deciding problem rather than the climbing.
hazards: Steep snow gullies on the traverse with a bad runout in early season
Wrong notch — U-notch on the left versus V-notch on the right
Bergschrunds flanking the snow tongue, ten to fifteen feet down to rock
Rockfall, natural and climber-triggered, on the upper gullies and staircase
Moat at the glacier-rock junction, worsening through the season and year on year
No camping permitted at Cascade Pass or on Mixup Arm

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass, Cache Col and Kool-Aid Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road, follow the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and roughly 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at about 5,400 ft. This stretch is well graded, well marked and by far the busiest — it is a popular day hike in its own right.

At the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up the climbers' path to climber's right, bearing south-southeast. It makes a rising traverse over snow or heather across the east flanks of Mixup Peak, crossing a spur ridge, to the base of the Cache Glacier at about 6,000 ft. The path is intermittent and in early season it is under snow, when route-finding matters more and the traverse has a bad runout.

Ascend moderate snow — up to about 35 degrees — to Cache Col at roughly 6,900-6,960 ft. The glacier here is small and generally reported free of significant crevasse hazard, but carry an axe and often crampons depending on firmness. Late season Cache Col itself can moat out and become awkward to cross.

From Cache Col make a descending traverse south-southeast, losing about 600 ft, to Kool-Aid Lake at about 6,120 ft — the standard camp for Magic Mountain and for the Ptarmigan Traverse, with reliable water. Most parties treat this as a two-day trip rather than a car-to-car push.

A Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking; overnight camping at Kool-Aid Lake needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, picked up in person at Marblemount for the Cascade River Road areas.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The South Ridge starts at the col between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up Peak, at about 7,100 ft. From Kool-Aid Lake it is roughly 1,000 ft of straightforward heather and scree straight up to that col — there is no gully to pick and no notch to confuse, which makes this the most forgiving base on this list to arrive at.

The route-finding problem is not the base but the top, and it is worth knowing before you set off. The first third of the ridge is an easy heather scramble, with possible snow, leading to a FALSE summit about 300 ft southeast of the true summit. That false summit is the landmark that tells you you are on route, and it is also where parties stop, believing they have topped out.

From the false summit the way on is counter-intuitive: find a dirty gully on the right and downclimb about 80 ft, then follow class 3-4 broken ledges that corkscrew around the east and northeast side of the summit tower. A hand line or a belay is worth having, and the descent goes back down the climbing route.

In poor visibility the two things to hold onto are that the col is the low point on the skyline between Magic and Hurry-Up, and that if you are standing on a high point with more rock still above you across a gap, you are on the false summit and need to lose height on the right before regaining it.
hazards: Snow-covered traverse below Mixup with a poor runout in early season
Cache Col moats out and becomes awkward late season
Loose rock on the summit tower ledges
The false summit — parties stop there or commit to the wrong side of it
No water on the upper ridge; last reliable source is Kool-Aid Lake
